questions.title: Define virtual reality
questions.text: Define the term **virtual reality**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A computer-generated 3D environment that completely replaces the user's view of the real world (1)
- in which the user feels immersed / can interact in real time, usually with a headset (1)

points.criterion: Computer-generated environment replacing the real view

scheme.model_answer: A computer-generated 3D environment that completely replaces what the user sees, so that, wearing a headset, they feel present in it and can interact with it.

questions.title: Define augmented reality
questions.text: Define the term **augmented reality**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Computer-generated content (images, text, 3D objects) is added / overlaid on the user's view of the real world (1)
- in real time; the real world remains visible (via phone camera / AR glasses) (1)

points.criterion: Digital content overlaid on the real world
Real time / real world still visible

scheme.model_answer: Technology that adds computer-generated images and information on top of the user's live view of the real world, which they can still see.

questions.title: VR vs AR
questions.text: Augmented reality and virtual reality technologies are gaining popularity. Explain the difference between virtual and augmented reality.

scheme.mark_scheme: A virtual reality replaces your vision, augmented reality adds to it (1). VR completely covers and replaces your field of vision; AR apps only show digital objects on top of the real world on your screen / glasses (1)

points.criterion: AR adds to the real view

scheme.model_answer: Virtual reality replaces the user's vision with a computer-generated world, whereas augmented reality adds digital objects on top of the real world that the user can still see.

questions.title: Which is AR?
questions.text: Which of these is an example of **augmented** reality?

options.content: A headset game set on a spaceship
A phone app that translates a street sign when the camera points at it
A flight simulator with a closed cockpit and screens
A 3D film watched in a cinema

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: The translation is drawn over the live camera view of the real sign.

questions.title: VR, AR or MR
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the technology used.

prefill: A headset tour of the International Space Station
Speed and directions shown on a car windscreen
A virtual robot that walks around a real table and hides behind a real sofa
Treating a fear of heights by standing on a virtual skyscraper

scheme.mark_scheme: Space station → VR (1); Windscreen → AR (1); Robot behind sofa → MR (1); Skyscraper therapy → VR (1)

questions.title: Purposes of AR
questions.text: State **two** purposes of augmented reality.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): provides real-time access to information / data / context relevant to the physical world; provides immersive and interactive learning experiences; try products before buying; navigation / directions; maintenance or repair instructions over equipment; guidance in surgery; entertainment / games; tourism information
scheme.model_answer: 1 To give real-time information about what the user is looking at, such as directions in a city. 2 To provide interactive learning, such as a 3D model of the heart on a textbook page.

questions.title: VR hardware
questions.text: Match each part of a VR system to its purpose.

right.text: Shows a separate image to each eye to create 3D depth
Track the movement and rotation of the user's head
Let the user point at and pick up virtual objects
Vibrations let the user feel contact with virtual objects

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: AR hardware
questions.text: Select **two** devices that can be used to experience augmented reality.

options.content: A closed VR headset that blocks all outside light
Smart glasses with a transparent display

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: How VR creates immersion
questions.text: Describe how a VR headset makes the user feel that they are really inside the virtual world.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): two screens / a different image for each eye give stereoscopic 3D; the display fills the field of view / blocks the real world; sensors track head movement and update the view instantly; high frame rate / low latency; controllers let the user interact; spatial audio; haptic feedback
scheme.model_answer: The headset shows a slightly different image to each eye, which creates 3D depth, and it blocks out the real world. Sensors track the user's head, so the view changes immediately when they look around, and spatial sound comes from the direction of virtual objects.

questions.title: How an AR app works
questions.text: Describe how an AR app on a phone shows a virtual lamp standing on a real table.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): camera captures live video; sensors / computer vision detect the table surface and the phone's position; the 3D model is anchored to the table; the lamp is drawn over the video at the correct size and angle; it is updated as the phone moves so it stays in place
scheme.model_answer: The camera captures live video of the room, and computer vision detects the flat surface of the table. The app anchors the 3D lamp to the table and draws it over the video at the right size; as the phone moves, sensors update the view so the lamp stays in place.

questions.title: Types of AR
questions.text: Match each type of AR to an example.

right.text: A 3D dinosaur appears when the camera sees a picture in a book
Game creatures appear at real places found using GPS
A virtual chair is placed on any floor the camera detects

scheme.mark_scheme: Marker–R1, Location–R2, Markerless–R3. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: VR for training
questions.text: Explain the purpose of virtual reality in training **firefighters**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Firefighters can practise entering burning buildings / rescues in a realistic simulation (1)
- without danger / cheaper than real fires / any scenario can be repeated (1)
scheme.model_answer: Firefighters can practise searching a burning building in a realistic virtual environment, without any real danger, and repeat the exercise as many times as needed.

questions.title: VR and AR in medicine
questions.text: State **one** purpose of VR and **one** purpose of AR in medicine.

scheme.mark_scheme:
VR (1): surgery practice / training; treating phobias / PTSD; pain distraction; rehabilitation exercises; explaining an operation to a patient
AR (1): showing veins / scans / organs over the patient's body during surgery; guiding injections; remote expert guidance; anatomy teaching on a real body
scheme.model_answer: VR: treating patients' fear of flying with a virtual flight. AR: showing a patient's CT scan over their body during an operation.

questions.title: AR in retail
questions.text: Explain how an online furniture shop can benefit from an AR app.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Customers can see a 3D model of the furniture in their own room at its real size (1)
- so they know it fits / matches before buying → more sales / fewer returns (1)

points.criterion: Try the product in the real room
Benefit: confidence / fewer returns / more sales

scheme.model_answer: Customers can place a life-size 3D model of a sofa in their own living room, so they can check that it fits and looks right before buying, which means fewer returns for the shop.

questions.title: Motion sickness
questions.text: Some users feel dizzy or sick when using VR, especially if the image is updated too slowly.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: A delay between head movement and the image (latency) or a low frame rate confuses the brain and causes motion sickness.

questions.title: Drawbacks
questions.text: State **one** drawback of VR and **one** drawback of AR.

scheme.mark_scheme:
VR (1): motion sickness / eye strain; isolated from surroundings / may bump into objects; expensive equipment; needs powerful computer
AR (1): distraction — dangerous while walking / driving; privacy — camera records surroundings; drains battery; small screen; tracking errors; AR glasses expensive
scheme.model_answer: VR: users cannot see the real room, so they may trip over furniture. AR: people may walk into traffic while looking at their phone.

questions.title: VR or AR for a school
questions.text:
A school has money to buy **either** 30 VR headsets **or** 30 tablets with AR apps for its science lessons.

Discuss which option the school should choose. Justify your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
VR (max 2): full immersion — virtual trips inside cells / to space; safe experiments; but expensive, motion sickness, isolates students / teacher cannot see what they see, limited time per lesson
AR (max 2): 3D models over textbooks / desk; students still see the teacher and each other — collaboration; tablets cheaper / multi-use; but less immersive, small screen
Justified conclusion (1)
[Max 4]

points.criterion: Valid point about VR in lessons
Valid point about AR in lessons

scheme.model_answer: VR headsets would give a fully immersive experience, such as travelling inside a cell, but they are expensive, can cause motion sickness and cut students off from the teacher. Tablets with AR show 3D models on top of the textbook while students can still see and talk to each other, and the tablets can be used for other tasks too. The school should choose the AR tablets because they are cheaper, more flexible and allow group work.

questions.title: Technology for tourists
questions.text: The tourist office in Turkestan wants to attract more visitors to the Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi.

parts.title: Location-based AR
parts.text: Explain how a **location-based** AR app could help visitors at the mausoleum.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The app uses GPS / compass to know where the visitor is and which part of the building they are looking at (1)
- and shows information / history / reconstructions / directions over the camera view (1)

points.criterion: Relevant content shown over the real view

scheme.model_answer: Using GPS, the app knows which part of the mausoleum the visitor is pointing the phone at and shows its history and a reconstruction of how it looked when it was built.

parts.title: VR tour
parts.text: Explain the purpose of offering a **VR** tour of the mausoleum on the tourist office's website.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- People who cannot travel can experience / explore the building in 3D from anywhere (1)
- it advertises the site so more people decide to visit / shows closed or fragile areas (1)

points.criterion: Benefit: attracts visitors / access to closed areas

scheme.model_answer: People anywhere in the world can explore the mausoleum in 3D, which advertises it and encourages them to come and visit in person.

parts.title: A risk
parts.text: Explain **one** problem visitors might have when using the AR app at the site.

scheme.mark_scheme: Problem (1) + explanation (1): distraction — visitors look at the screen and trip / walk into others; battery drains quickly; weak GPS / mobile signal so content appears in the wrong place; small screen hard to see in bright sunlight
scheme.model_answer: In bright sunlight the phone screen is hard to see, and visitors who keep looking at it may trip on the steps.

questions.title: Evaluate VR and AR
questions.text: Evaluate the use of virtual reality and augmented reality in **education and training**. Refer to specific examples.

scheme.mark_scheme:
VR (max 3): purpose / example (simulators for pilots, surgeons; virtual field trips) (1); benefits — safe, cheaper, repeatable, engaging (1); drawbacks — cost, motion sickness, isolation (1)
AR (max 3): purpose / example (3D models over textbooks, instructions over machines) (1); benefits — real world visible, cheap on phones, collaboration (1); drawbacks — distraction, small screen, less immersive (1)
A conclusion may gain credit within the maximum.
scheme.model_answer: VR is used for simulators in which pilots and surgeons practise dangerous procedures. This is safe, cheaper than real practice and can be repeated, but headsets are expensive, some users feel sick and they are cut off from the real world. AR is used to show 3D models of organs or planets over textbooks and instructions over real machines. Learners still see the real world and can work together, and it runs on phones most people already own, but it is less immersive and the small screen can be distracting. VR is best for realistic practice of dangerous tasks, and AR for everyday classroom learning.

questions.title: VR and AR
questions.text: Augmented reality and virtual reality technologies are gaining popularity.

parts.title: Difference
parts.text: Explain the difference between virtual and augmented reality.

scheme.mark_scheme: A virtual reality replaces your vision, augmented reality adds to it (1). VR completely covers and replaces your field of vision; AR apps show digital objects on top of the real world on a screen / glasses (1)

points.criterion: AR adds to the real view

scheme.model_answer: Virtual reality replaces what the user sees with a computer-generated world, while augmented reality adds digital objects to the user's view of the real world.

parts.title: Which technology
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the application uses VR or AR.

prefill: Trying on virtual glasses using the front camera of a phone
A driving simulator for learner drivers
Arrows on the camera view guiding a visitor through an airport

scheme.mark_scheme: Glasses → AR (1); Driving simulator → VR (1); Airport arrows → AR (1)

Any two (1 each): AR provides real-time access to information, data and context relevant to the physical world; provides immersive and interactive learning experiences; try before you buy; navigation; repair / maintenance instructions; surgical guidance; entertainment
scheme.model_answer: 1 To give real-time information about objects in the physical world, such as translating a menu. 2 To provide interactive learning experiences, such as 3D models in a textbook.

parts.title: AR hardware
parts.text: State **one** device that can be used to display augmented reality.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): smartphone; tablet; AR / smart glasses; head-up display; mixed-reality headset (HoloLens)
scheme.model_answer: A smartphone with a camera.

questions.title: Training and medicine
questions.text: A regional hospital uses VR headsets to train junior surgeons and AR glasses during real operations.

parts.title: Purpose of VR
parts.text: Explain the purpose of using VR to train the junior surgeons.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- They practise operations in a realistic simulated environment (1)
- without risk to patients / mistakes can be made and repeated / rare cases can be practised (1)
scheme.model_answer: Junior surgeons can practise operations on virtual patients, making and learning from mistakes without any risk to real people.

parts.title: Immersion
parts.text: Describe **two** features of a VR headset that make the training feel realistic.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): separate image for each eye — 3D depth; head tracking updates the view; blocks out the real world / wide field of view; hand controllers / gloves to handle instruments; haptic feedback; spatial sound; high frame rate
scheme.model_answer: It shows a different image to each eye to create 3D depth, and it tracks the surgeon's head so the view of the virtual patient changes as they move.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): expensive headsets / software; motion sickness / eye strain; cannot fully reproduce touch / resistance of real tissue; isolates the user; needs powerful computers / maintenance
scheme.model_answer: 1 The equipment and software are expensive. 2 It cannot reproduce exactly how real tissue feels.

parts.title: AR in surgery
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the AR glasses during real operations.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Scans / veins / organs / patient data are shown over the surgeon's view of the patient (1)
- so the surgeon can see inside without looking away at a screen / operates more accurately (1)

points.criterion: Benefit: accuracy / no need to look away

scheme.model_answer: The glasses show the patient's CT scan over their body, so the surgeon can see exactly where the organs are without looking away at a monitor.

questions.title: Shops and museums
questions.text: A furniture shop and a city museum both want to use new reality technologies.

parts.title: Furniture AR app
parts.text: Describe how the shop's AR app lets a customer see a wardrobe in their bedroom.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): camera shows live view of the room; sensors / computer vision detect floor and walls; 3D model of the wardrobe anchored to the floor; drawn over the live view at real size; stays in place as the phone moves
scheme.model_answer: The phone camera shows the bedroom, computer vision detects the floor, and the app places a life-size 3D model of the wardrobe on it, which stays in the same place as the customer moves around.

parts.title: Benefit to the shop
parts.text: Explain **one** benefit to the shop of this app.

scheme.mark_scheme: Benefit (1) + explanation (1): fewer returns because customers know it fits; more sales / customers buy online with confidence; smaller showroom needed
scheme.model_answer: Fewer items are returned, because customers can check that the wardrobe fits and matches the room before buying.

parts.title: Museum choice
parts.text: Discuss whether the museum should use VR or AR to show visitors how the ancient city of Otrar looked 800 years ago.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 3 marks:
- VR: visitors could walk through a full 3D reconstruction of the city — very immersive (1); but headsets expensive / one visitor at a time / sickness (1)
- AR: reconstruction shown over real ruins / exhibits on phones — visitors see the real artefacts too (1); less immersive (1)
- Justified conclusion (1)
[Max 3]
scheme.model_answer: VR would let visitors walk through the whole city as it looked 800 years ago, which is very immersive, but only a few visitors could use the headsets at a time. AR would show the reconstruction on top of the real ruins and artefacts using visitors' own phones. VR is better here because the city no longer exists, so a complete virtual reconstruction shows it best.

summary: The purpose of virtual and augmented reality — how VR and AR work, the hardware they use, the difference between them and mixed reality, their uses in education, medicine, industry, retail and entertainment, and their benefits and drawbacks.

blocks.content: A **computer-generated, three-dimensional environment** that **completely replaces** the user's view of the real world. Using a headset, the user feels **immersed** (present) in the virtual world and can **interact** with it in real time.

Technology that **overlays computer-generated content** — text, images, 3D models, sound — **onto the user's view of the real world in real time**. The real world remains visible; it is **enhanced (augmented)** with digital information.

A combination in which **virtual objects are anchored in the real world and interact with it** — for example, a virtual ball that bounces off a real table and can be hidden behind a real chair. Example device: Microsoft HoloLens, Apple Vision Pro.

REAL WORLD ------- AUGMENTED REALITY ------- MIXED REALITY ------- VIRTUAL REALITY
everything real    digital layer on top      digital objects      everything is
                   of the real view          interact with        computer-generated
                   (phone, AR glasses)       real ones            (VR headset)

blocks.content: **Virtual reality replaces your vision; augmented reality adds to it.**

items.title: Head-mounted display (HMD)
items.content: Two small screens (one for each eye) show slightly different images, creating **stereoscopic 3D** depth. Lenses make the image fill the field of view.

items.title: Tracking
items.content: **Gyroscopes, accelerometers** and cameras track the position and rotation of the head (**six degrees of freedom**), so the view changes instantly when the user looks around or walks.

items.title: Controllers and gloves
items.content: Hand-held controllers or data gloves track the hands, so the user can **pick up, push and point** at virtual objects.

items.title: Haptic feedback
items.content: Vibrations (and in advanced systems, force feedback) let the user **feel** contact with virtual objects.

items.title: Spatial audio
items.content: Sound changes with the direction of the user's head, adding to the feeling of presence.

items.title: Powerful processing
items.content: A computer, console or the headset itself must render **two high-resolution images at 90+ frames per second** with **very low latency**; otherwise users feel **motion sickness**.

blocks.content:
flowchart TB
  S[Sensors track head and hands] --> C[Computer updates the virtual scene]
  C --> R[Renders an image for each eye]
  R --> D[Headset displays the images]
  D --> S
blocks.caption: The VR loop runs many times per second

blocks.title: How an AR app places a virtual sofa in your room
items: The **camera** captures live video of the room.
**Sensors** (gyroscope, accelerometer, depth sensor, GPS) and **computer vision** detect the floor, walls and the device's position (this mapping is called **SLAM**).
The app **anchors** a 3D model of the sofa to the floor at the chosen spot.
The model is **drawn on top of the live video** at the correct size and angle; as the user moves, it stays in place.

columns: How it decides where to show content
rows: Recognises a printed image / QR code
Pointing a tablet at a textbook page shows a 3D heart
Detects surfaces (floors, tables) with computer vision
Pokémon GO; arrows for walking directions; information about a building
Projected keyboards; assembly instructions projected onto a workbench
Information shown on a transparent screen / windscreen
Speed and navigation on a car windscreen; pilots' HUD

theory.title: The purpose of VR and AR in different fields

blocks.title: Purposes by field
rows: Virtual field trips (space, ancient Rome, inside a cell); safe science experiments
3D models on top of textbooks; labelled anatomy; star maps; interactive learning
**Simulators** for pilots, drivers, surgeons, soldiers, firefighters — practise dangerous situations safely
Step-by-step instructions shown on real equipment during training
Surgery practice; treating **phobias** and PTSD (exposure therapy); pain distraction; rehabilitation
Showing a patient's veins / scans **over the body** during an operation
Walking through a building or car **before it is built**; testing designs
Seeing a planned building at its real location; maintenance instructions over machines
**Try before you buy** — furniture in your room, glasses or make-up on your face
Virtual tours of museums and cities
Information and reconstructions over ruins and exhibits
Location-based games, camera filters, live sports graphics
Directions over the street view; car HUDs
Remote experts draw instructions onto a worker's live view

blocks.title: Purposes of AR (exam style)
blocks.content: AR provides **real-time access to information** relevant to what the user is looking at in the physical world (e.g. translating a sign, showing the name of a building), and provides **immersive and interactive learning experiences** (e.g. a 3D volcano erupting on the desk).

blocks.title: Purpose of VR in pilot training
blocks.content: Trainee pilots practise take-offs, landings and **emergencies** (engine failure, storms) in a realistic virtual cockpit. There is **no danger** to people or aircraft, it is **cheaper** than real flights, and any situation can be **repeated** as often as needed.

items.title: Benefits of VR
items.content:
- Safe practice of **dangerous** or **rare** situations.
- **Cheaper** than real training (fuel, equipment, travel).
- Experiences that are **impossible** in reality (inside the human body, other planets).
- Very **engaging** — learners remember more.

items.title: Drawbacks of VR
items.content:
- **Motion sickness**, eye strain and headaches; not suitable for young children for long periods.
- Users are **isolated** from the real world and can **bump into objects**.
- **Expensive** headsets and powerful computers.
- May not feel completely realistic (no real touch, weight).

items.title: Benefits of AR
items.content:
- Users stay **aware of the real world** — safer, can be used while walking or working.
- Works on **smartphones** that many people already own — cheap and accessible.
- Gives **information at the moment it is needed**, in context.

items.title: Drawbacks of AR
items.content:
- **Distraction** — dangerous if people look at the screen while walking or driving.
- **Privacy** — the camera constantly records the surroundings.
- Small phone screens; AR glasses are expensive; drains the **battery**.
- Tracking errors make virtual objects drift or appear in the wrong place.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain the difference between virtual and augmented reality. [2]**
A virtual reality **replaces** your vision, augmented reality **adds to** it (1). VR completely covers and replaces the field of vision with a computer-generated world, while AR shows digital objects **on top of the real world**, seen through a screen or glasses (1).

**Q: State two purposes of augmented reality. [2]**
To give **real-time access to information** about the physical world around the user (1); to provide **immersive and interactive learning** experiences (1). *(Also: try products before buying, navigation, maintenance instructions.)*

**Q: Explain one purpose of virtual reality in medicine. [2]**
Surgeons can **practise operations** in a realistic virtual environment (1) **without any risk** to real patients (1).

- Saying AR "creates a virtual world" — AR **adds** to the **real** world; only VR creates a whole virtual world.
- Describing VR/AR only by the device ("you wear a headset") without stating its **purpose**.
- Giving a purpose without the **benefit** — say *why* VR training is better (safe, cheaper, repeatable).
- Confusing a **360° video** (you can only look around) with full VR (you can also interact).
